basic_identification.name: Provenance tracking systems
basic_identification.originator: Verisart (Robert Norton, 2015), Artory (Nanne Dekking, 2016), blockchain-native records via Ethereum/Bitcoin. Also: Codex Protocol, Everledger, Tagsmart. Institutional precedents from Christie's, Sotheby's partnership with Artory.
basic_identification.year: 2015-2016 (blockchain-specific); provenance tracking as practice dates to early modern art market
basic_identification.geography: Global. Verisart (Los Angeles/London), Artory (New York/Berlin). Adoption strongest in US, Europe, with emerging interest in Asia-Pacific.

core_ideas.core_claim: Blockchain-based provenance systems create immutable, verifiable records of artwork authenticity and ownership history, addressing the art market's longstanding problem of forged or incomplete provenance. Verisart uses Bitcoin blockchain for digital certificates; Artory creates secure digital registrations consolidating fragmented records into single verifiable entries.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Bridges physical and digital art worlds. For physical art, these systems digitize traditionally paper-based provenance records. For digital/NFT art, on-chain provenance is native. The blockchain-specific innovation is immutability: once recorded, provenance cannot be retroactively altered, addressing an estimated 50% forgery rate in circulating art.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Primarily infrastructure-neutral. Provenance tracking serves verification rather than engagement. However, provenance increasingly functions as a marketing tool in NFT markets where chain of ownership (especially celebrity or notable collector provenance) drives speculative attention. The attention economy co-opts provenance as a status signal rather than a knowledge resource.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Intention-aligned at the design level: provenance tracking serves a declared structural need of the field (authentication, trust, knowledge). In practice, the implementation has been mixed: some systems serve institutional verification needs (intention), while the NFT ecosystem weaponizes provenance as a speculation signal (attention). The gap between provenance of ownership and provenance of meaning remains unaddressed.

market_economics.revenue_model: Verisart: freemium model with paid certification tiers for artists and galleries. Artory: B2B partnerships with auction houses and institutions. Codex Protocol: token-based (CODX). Broader market: the digital art authentication market was valued at approximately $360M in 2025, projected to reach $4.8B by 2032 at 38.7% CAGR.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure layer between creators/collectors and marketplaces. Sits alongside rather than competing with trading platforms.
market_economics.price_range: Certification costs range from free (basic Verisart) to institutional pricing for auction house integrations. Not a direct art sales platform.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing. The digital art authentication market is expanding rapidly despite the NFT crash, driven by institutional adoption and traditional art world integration. European adoption leads due to established art markets; North America is fastest-growing due to NFT ecosystem. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: Mixed: traditional art collectors seeking authentication for physical works, crypto-native collectors for NFT provenance, institutional buyers (museums, auction houses) for compliance and due diligence. Increasingly serving luxury goods and fashion provenance beyond art. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: More sustainable than speculative NFT markets because provenance tracking addresses a permanent structural need. Authentication demand exists regardless of market cycles. B2B models (Artory with Christie's) provide recurring revenue independent of art price levels. The challenge is building network effects: a provenance system is only valuable if widely adopted.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Bitcoin blockchain (Verisart), Ethereum (various), proprietary databases with blockchain anchoring, IPFS for certificate storage, QR codes linking physical objects to digital records, mobile apps for verification scanning, API integrations with gallery management software.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Emerging intersection. AI is used for visual authentication (comparing artworks to known databases), detecting forgeries through style analysis, and automating metadata extraction. Provenance systems could theoretically track whether a work was AI-generated or AI-assisted, but this is not yet standard. AI training data provenance (tracking what data models were trained on) is a parallel concern addressed by different tools (Spawning).
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Primarily archival: provenance records are cumulative, append-only logs. Some real-time elements emerge with blockchain-native art where provenance is updated with each transaction. Not performative or generative.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Provenance vocabulary is market/legal rather than aesthetic: certificate of authenticity, chain of custody, title transfer, exhibition history, condition report, catalogue raisonne. The vocabulary for provenance of meaning (interpretation history, critical reception, contextual evolution) barely exists. This vocabulary gap is a key finding.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Infrastructure over spectacle. Mixed on openness: blockchain records are transparent but proprietary systems enclose data. Commons-adjacent when records are public; capture-adjacent when locked in proprietary databases. Individual ownership model, not collective.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Mixed. On-chain provenance records are transparent by default. However, proprietary systems (Artory, Verisart) enclose their databases and certification processes. Verisart uses Bitcoin blockchain (open) with proprietary verification layers. No universal open standard for art provenance data.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Corporate/founding-team for individual platforms. No industry-wide governance body for provenance standards. The art market's decentralized nature means no single authority can mandate adoption. Museums follow institutional conservation standards (CIDOC-CRM) that predate blockchain.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Problematic. In proprietary systems, artists and collectors depend on the platform's continued operation. If Verisart or Artory shut down, what happens to the certificates? On-chain records persist but the verification interface may not. Data portability between provenance systems is poor. Artists cannot easily export their full provenance history from one system to another.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low. No universal provenance data standard connects Verisart, Artory, Codex, and on-chain NFT records. Each system uses its own data model. The CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model exists for museum objects but is not widely adopted in the blockchain provenance space. Getty vocabularies (ULAN, AAT) could provide shared ontology but are not integrated.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Blockchain-anchored records are preserved as long as the chain operates. Proprietary platform data is at-risk if companies fail. IPFS-pinned certificates depend on pinning. Physical certificate backups vary. No standardized preservation mandate across the industry.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Minimal. Provenance recording is typically initiated by the creator or current owner. No mechanism for an artwork's subjects (e.g., photographed individuals) to consent to or contest provenance records. No machine-readable consent layer for how provenance data itself may be used or shared.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Integration is the goal. Artory's partnership with Christie's for the Barney A. Ebsworth Collection represented a milestone in traditional auction house adoption. Museums are experimenting (Louvre exploring blockchain for restoration history). However, adoption remains slow in the traditional art world, which relies on established dealer relationships and connoisseurship rather than technological verification.
field_position.what_it_enables: Verifiable, tamper-proof ownership records accessible to anyone. Democratization of authentication (artists can self-certify without gallery intermediaries). Faster due diligence for collectors. Potential for automating royalty payments on secondary sales. Cross-border provenance verification without relying on local intermediaries.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Provenance of meaning. Current systems track ownership transfers but not interpretation history, exhibition context, critical reception, conservation decisions, or evolving significance. There is no standard for recording why a work matters, only who owned it. Also lacks: retroactive verification of pre-digital provenance, interoperability between systems, privacy-preserving verification (anonymous collectors), and mechanisms for contested provenance (looted art, colonial heritage).
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists without digital literacy or blockchain access. Markets in regions with limited internet infrastructure. Artists whose work is collaborative, ephemeral, or process-based (provenance systems assume discrete ownable objects). Indigenous and non-Western art traditions where Western provenance concepts may not apply. Collectors who require anonymity (privacy tension with transparency).
field_position.frontier_signal: Established concept, frontier implementation. The idea of blockchain provenance is well-understood. The frontier is in expanding from ownership provenance to meaning provenance, achieving cross-platform interoperability, and integrating AI-powered authentication. The market is growing but consolidation has not occurred.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: B2B partnerships and institutional adoption rather than consumer marketing. Word of mouth among galleries, auction houses, and collectors. Industry conferences. Some social media presence but not attention-dependent.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Low. Provenance tracking serves functional verification needs independent of social media attention. Would survive platform disappearance. However, the NFT-adjacent provenance market is somewhat attention-dependent through association with crypto culture.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Strongly intention-aligned in purpose: serves a declared structural need for authentication and trust. Implementation varies: institutional use (Artory/Christie's) is intention-native; NFT marketplace provenance display can be attention-native (provenance as flex).
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Mixed. On-chain records are public commons by default. Proprietary databases enclose provenance knowledge. No major initiative to create open, shared provenance infrastructure for the art field. The data that would be most valuable to the commons (interconnected provenance across collections) remains fragmented and proprietary.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Ownership only. Current systems excel at tracking chain of custody but do not track provenance of meaning, interpretation, or contextual evolution. This is the central limitation from an A(DAI) perspective.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Archival and cumulative. Records append over time. No cyclical, anticipatory, or deep-historical logic. The temporal model is a linear chain of transfers, which misses the non-linear ways artworks accumulate meaning.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: Does not address absence systematically. Pre-digital provenance gaps remain unverifiable. Lost or destroyed works leave no trace. Periods of unknown ownership (lacunae) are recorded as gaps but not analyzed. There is no mechanism for representing what is missing from the provenance record or why it matters.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Consensus-seeking: provenance systems aim for a single authoritative record of ownership. Multiple conflicting provenance claims are treated as errors to be resolved, not as coexisting valid interpretations. This consensus model works for ownership but breaks down for meaning, where multiple valid readings should coexist.
coherence.contestability: Limited. Blockchain records are immutable by design, making contestation technically difficult. Disputed provenance (especially for looted or colonially acquired art) creates real tension: the technology's strength (immutability) becomes a weakness when records need correction or recontextualization. Some systems allow annotations but not modifications to core records.
coherence.forkability: Technically forkable: open-source tools and public blockchain data can be replicated. Practically difficult because provenance value comes from institutional trust and network adoption. A forked provenance system without Christie's or major gallery backing would lack credibility.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The immutable record principle: once provenance is established, it should not be silently altered. The append-only model for building cumulative knowledge. The ambition to make verification accessible without intermediaries. The partnership model for institutional adoption (Artory/Christie's approach). The recognition that provenance is foundational infrastructure, not a feature.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The ownership-only model that reduces provenance to chain of custody. The consensus-seeking approach that eliminates legitimate disagreement. The proprietary database model that encloses provenance knowledge. The assumption that provenance is a linear chain rather than a branching, contextual network. The neglect of absence: what is missing from a provenance record is as important as what is present.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Provenance tracking systems answer 'who owned this?' A(DAI) needs to answer 'what does this mean and how has that meaning changed?' The ownership layer is necessary but radically insufficient. The productive tension is that A(DAI) can build meaning provenance on top of (or alongside) ownership provenance, creating a richer, multi-dimensional record that includes interpretation, exhibition context, critical reception, and evolving significance. The challenge is that the field currently equates 'provenance' with 'ownership' and has no vocabulary for meaning provenance.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Increasing regulatory interest. EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives require provenance verification for high-value art transactions. The EU AI Act indirectly affects AI-powered authentication tools. GDPR creates tension with public blockchain records (right to be forgotten vs. immutability). Cultural property laws (UNESCO Convention, national patrimony laws) intersect with provenance systems for restitution claims. No specific regulation mandates blockchain provenance but due diligence requirements are tightening.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Provenance records themselves are typically treated as factual data (not copyrightable). The platforms' database structures and verification methods may be proprietary. Artwork metadata in provenance records raises questions about database rights (EU sui generis database right). No clear IP model for shared provenance data.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in: artists and collectors voluntarily register works. No mandatory provenance registration exists in most jurisdictions. This creates a fragmented landscape where provenance is available for some works and absent for others.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Verisart depends on Bitcoin blockchain and its own servers. Artory depends on Ethereum and proprietary infrastructure. Both depend on art market relationships and institutional partnerships. No single point of failure at the blockchain layer, but significant dependency on the companies' continued operation for verification interfaces.
ecosystem.network_effects: Moderate positive network effects: a provenance system becomes more valuable as more participants use it. However, the network is fragmented across competing systems with no interoperability. The art market's relationship-driven nature means network effects operate through institutional trust rather than pure scale.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Growing independently of NFT market cycles. The need for art authentication is countercyclical (higher scrutiny in down markets). The digital art authentication market is projected to grow from $360M (2025) to $4.8B (2032). Blockchain provenance is becoming accepted infrastructure rather than a speculative novelty. The post-crash period has been positive for provenance systems as the field shifts from speculation to utility.
